title: Backend Web Development Explained
summary: Defines full-stack development and splits a web app into frontend and backend, with the backend made of server, application and database. Walks through the request/response cycle with a login example and a restaurant comparison.

concepts.heading: Why full-stack
points: Early startup roles favour people who can build things; job listings for startups mostly ask for full-stack developers.
Full-stack means handling both the client-facing frontend and the invisible backend that holds the application logic.

concepts.heading: Frontend vs backend
points: Frontend: everything a user can see, hear or interact with (fonts, colours, buttons, forms).
Backend: what the user never sees or touches; it makes the app function.

concepts.heading: The three backend parts
points: Server: a computer that stays on and listens for browser requests. Any networked machine can be a server; during development localhost makes your own computer the server.

Application: code running on the server that decides how to answer each request. It can return an HTML page, data, or only a status code such as 404, which signals that the request is not something the app knows how to handle.
Database: persistent storage for user data. Without one, data held only in memory is lost when the machine loses power. Not every app needs one, but larger apps usually do.

concepts.heading: Website vs web application
points: So far the course built static sites: HTML, CSS and JS files stored somewhere (e.g. GitHub Pages) and returned unchanged on request.

A web app does more than show pages. Login is the simple example: the browser sends email and password in a request; the server routes it to login logic (e.g. a login.js); the app looks up the email in the database, compares passwords, and responds with the home page on a match or the login page again (with an error) otherwise.

concepts.heading: Restaurant comparison
points: Diner = client, menu = available interactions, waiter = the request/response carrier, kitchen = server, chef = application with recipes, pantry = database, plated dish = the response (HTML, CSS, JS or data).
The request/response loop repeats for every new action.

pitfalls: A static site hosted on GitHub Pages has no backend logic, so it cannot do login or store data by itself.
(Extra) Real apps never store or compare plain-text passwords; this is covered in the authentication section.

gaps_and_ideas: Proposed new lesson 'Frontend vs backend'. Blurb: the frontend is what the user sees and clicks; the backend is a server that listens for requests, an application that decides the response, and a database that keeps data between sessions.

Tasks: (1) drag labels (client, server, application, database) onto a diagram; (2) sort a list of items (button colour, password check, saved user list, font) into frontend or backend; (3) trace a login request step by step and pick the response for a correct and an incorrect password; (4) match status codes 200, 404 and 401 to their meaning.

Starter code idea: the in-memory handleLogin() function above, editable in the lesson, with a form whose submit calls it and prints the returned status/page, so learners can add a user or change the logic.

Interactive demo: an animated request/response loop where pressing Log in sends a packet from the browser to the server, into the application, to the database and back, with a toggle that switches to a static GitHub Pages site to show the request returning the same file with no logic or database step.
